Génocide à Gaza : fait ou opinion médiat: Genocide in Gaza: Fact or Media Opinion?
Des Gazaouis et experts analysent l’usag: Gazans and experts examine the use of the word “genocide” in the media, and its legal and ethical implications.

Alors que certains médias qualifient les: While some media outlets describe the massacres in Gaza as “genocide,” others refuse to, citing journalistic ethics among other considerations. In the industry, in Quebec as elsewhere in the West, many journalists and outlets are waiting for the International Court of Justice to rule on the matter. In this context, some are asking why the media are still waiting for such a judicial finding when there are images and testimonies, and statements from international NGOs. En plus d’être journaliste-recherchiste: In addition to being a journalist-researcher at La Converse, I’m a lawyer specializing in international human rights law. <strong>Les Gazaouis le répètent depuis: Gazans have been saying it for months: what they are enduring is a genocide. For months, the bombings, the targeted attacks on civilians and the famine have followed one another and accelerated.
<strong><em>Le 29 juillet, l’autorité in: On July 29, the leading international authority on food crises issued a new alert: the “worst-case scenario of famine” is currently unfolding in the Gaza Strip. On July 13, former Israeli prime minister Ehud Olmert spoke of the possible construction of a concentration camp in the Palestinian territory. Despite all this, the term “genocide” is still rarely used in mainstream media. Journalistic rigour in the face of a term that is “too loaded,” waiting for a legal ruling from the International Court of Justice – the reasons given are many. Meanwhile, the dead pile up, the destruction intensifies, the dehumanizing rhetoric multiplies, and the signs of a genocide are there.

Pour qu’un génocide soit reconnu légalem: For a genocide to be legally recognized, <l1>a court must rule on it</l1>. The bodies empowered to try individuals for this type of crime include the International Criminal Court (ICC), the ad hoc international criminal tribunals set up by the UN Security Council, and the national courts of member states. The International Court of Justice (ICJ), for its part, has jurisdiction to settle disputes between states. It can therefore be seized by a state in connection with a complaint about a potential genocide committed by another member state.

And if you’re a signatory to the Genocide Convention, you have to act to end it. So states avoid using the term, which is very problematic,” she hammers home.

Elle observe également une reprise massi: She also observes a massive adoption of the Israeli version of events, centred on the need to eradicate terrorism. “Newsrooms fell in line with that narrative instead of questioning state violence,” she laments. At the same time, “academics were told not to speak to the media.”
L’experte insiste sur la puissance de la: The expert stresses the power of Israeli propaganda, which is part, she tells us, of an effort to deny and destroy the intelligentsia on the ground: “The Israeli government has an extremely sophisticated propaganda machine, both on social media and within diaspora communities.”
À cela s’ajoutent les efforts d’Israël p: To this are added Israel’s efforts to discredit UN bodies on the ground. <l1>UNRWA, in particular, has been banned from operating in certain areas,</l1> which prevents it from documenting the abuses under way, even though it may have been collecting evidence of a possible genocide.
Elle se souvient d’une question posée en: She recalls a question put in 1994 by journalist Alan Elsner to a U.S. representative about Rwanda: “<l1>How many acts of genocide does it take to constitute genocide</l1>?”
« Et c’est ça, le problème : essayer de: “And that’s the problem: trying to gather the evidence. But when do we decide it’s enough?” asks Georgina Holmes, before concluding: “But it’s too late for the Palestinians…”
En 1994, au moment où les massacres comm: In 1994, when the massacres began in Rwanda, the BBC instructed its journalists to cover only what was happening at the country’s borders. “They were told it would be too dangerous to enter Rwanda, and that it was just a tribal conflict,” the researcher explains.
Mais en arrivant à la frontière du pays,: But on arriving at the border, the journalists were confronted with accounts that contradicted that interpretation of events. Survivors and aid workers described the atrocities they had suffered or witnessed. They struggled to describe the violence they had lived through, so unimaginable was it.
Malgré l’interdiction de leur hiérarchie: Despite their superiors’ ban, several BBC journalists then decided to enter Rwandan territory on their own. They began extensive documentation work, which would later serve as evidence in proceedings before the International Criminal Tribunal for Rwanda, the expert tells us.
Pourtant, même face à l’ampleur du drame: Yet even in the face of the scale of the tragedy, the journalists were forbidden by their superiors from using the term “genocide.” They then tried to document the unfolding of the Rwandan tragedy through the testimonies and images they gathered. “They were filming things that showed a genocide was under way. Piles of shoes, like those found in the Nazi camps. Children behind barbed wire in terrifying camps… They did everything they could to demonstrate that the incident was politically motivated and that it was state violence, not a tribal conflict.”
Malgré leurs efforts, le récit dominant: Despite their efforts, the dominant narrative in the media continued to present the situation as a conflict between neighbours, a spontaneous ethnic war, with no state orchestration. The tenacity of those few journalists on the ground would nevertheless end up tipping the scales: it was indeed a genocide, premeditated and sanctioned by government authorities.
Contrairement à la prudence éditoriale o: In contrast to the editorial caution seen over Rwanda, some journalists elsewhere chose to name what they were seeing very early on. Such is the case of Roy Gutman, an 81-year-old American reporter. Working for the newspaper Newsday, he was sent to Bosnia in 1992 to cover the Srebrenica genocide, which the world was then calling “an ethnic conflict.” He quickly understood that the situation on the ground went far beyond that simplistic narrative.
« Non, je ne croyais pas que c’était une: “No, I didn’t believe it was a simple war. I knew it was an enormous atrocity presented as a war,” he says.
Les premiers mois, le journaliste rappor: In the first few months, the journalist reported on mass deportations. But when he learned, through a local newspaper, that people were reportedly being taken to concentration camps, he decided to check whether those camps really existed.
What he discovered would haunt him for a long time. The camps did indeed exist. He collected accounts from civilians: systematic rape of women, summary executions, arbitrary detention.
« J’ai passé énormément de temps à recon: “I spent an enormous amount of time piecing together the big picture. I put all these stories side by side and at a certain point I said to myself: ‘Wait a second... There’s a pattern: deliberate expulsion of the population, dehumanization, extermination. Isn’t that precisely the definition of genocide?’ It was from these individual accounts that I gradually built that overall picture,” he explains.
Aucune instance juridique ne qualifie al: No legal body was calling these atrocities genocide at the time. But Roy Gutman wrote. He decided to name what he saw – a genocide – as early as 1992. In 1993, he published the book A Witness to Genocide, a collection of his articles on the subject. The book earned him the Pulitzer Prize the following year.
Plus tard, son travail, essentiel pour m: Later, his work, essential in bringing these crimes to light, would be cited in proceedings before the International Criminal Tribunal for the former Yugoslavia.
Aujourd’hui, à Gaza, la question demeure: Today, in Gaza, the question remains the same: “At what point does the accumulation of facts become sufficient for us to dare to name what we see?”
<strong>Attendre un verdict des tribunau: Waiting for a court verdict? The case of Srebrenica
Léo Kalinda, journaliste à la retraite q: Léo Kalinda, a retired journalist who had a long career at Radio-Canada, doesn’t mince words. He covered the genocide against the Tutsi in Rwanda and the one in Srebrenica, Bosnia.
Selon lui, compter sur la justice pour s: In his view, counting on the courts to rule on whether something qualifies as genocide is an illusion. The example of Srebrenica is proof: 30 years after the events, the debate is still heated.
En juillet 1995, plus de 8 000 hommes et: In July 1995, more than 8,000 Bosnian Muslim men and boys were executed by the Bosnian Serb army. The majority of <l1>women, children </l1>and elderly people, meanwhile, were spared. A planned and documented massacre. Yet international consensus was slow to emerge.
En 2015, une résolution du Royaume-Uni à: In 2015, a United Kingdom resolution at the UN to recognize this crime as a genocide was blocked by Russia, an ally of Serbia. The result: no UN recognition of the Srebrenica genocide.
Pourtant, la Cour internationale de just: Yet the International Court of Justice itself ruled in 2007: yes, it is a genocide.
Et ce flou persiste même parmi les spéci: And this blurriness persists even among specialists, explains Léo Kalinda. He recalls in particular D<sup>r</sup> Rony Brauman, a humanitarian who worked for many years with Médecins sans Frontières. <l1>According to him</l1>, there was a terrible massacre at Srebrenica, which amounts to a crime against humanity. But since women, children, elderly people and others who were not considered potential threats were allowed to leave, it was not a genocide.
Face à ces voix discordantes, Léo Kalind: Faced with these discordant voices, Léo Kalinda draws a lesson: “You see: even the specialists don’t agree.”
<strong>« Il y a des jours où je pense v: “There are days when I think I’m seeing images of Kigali in Gaza”
« Quand on regarde maintenant ce qui se: “When you look at what’s happening in Gaza now, it’s a repeat, 30 years later, of what happened in Rwanda,” he continues in a grave voice. (...) There are days when I think I’m seeing images of Kigali in Gaza.”
Il se souvient de ces scènes absurdes, «: He remembers those absurd scenes, “all those guys killing indiscriminately. In Rwanda, they shot at dogs, at anything.”
Léo Kalinda et ses collègues journaliste: Léo Kalinda and his fellow journalists had to hide from the Hutu army, in United Nations armoured vehicles, to document the unspeakable.
Aujourd’hui, il observe les mêmes méthod: Today, he sees the same methods used in Gaza by the Israeli army: the checkpoints, the generalized suspicion, the risks. “I see exactly what the Israeli army is doing: body searches of everyone who isn’t Israeli. It was strictly the same [in Rwanda].”
<strong>« Je trouve que le politiquement: “I think political correctness has its limits”
Les expériences de Léo Kalinda lui ont p: Léo Kalinda’s experiences have shaped a conviction: in the face of mass violence, euphemisms have no place. “Today, if I were on air, if Radio-Canada management said to me, ‘Listen, we’re going to take stock of Gaza, what do you think?’, I would definitely talk about genocide. (...) I think political correctness has its limits,” he says flatly.
<l1>Il note une autocensure médiatique n: <l1>He notes a self-censorship in the media fuelled by the fear of feeding antisemitism.</l1> This fear, he explains, paralyzes even public media: Radio-Canada and RFI, in particular, are said to be skittish because they anticipate the reactions of their readers and listeners. The former reporter believes that the use of the term “genocide” remains explosive.
« Dire qu’il y a un génocide à Gaza, ce: “Saying there is a genocide in Gaza is not at all saying – not even for three seconds – that you’re pro-Hamas. And you can list the facts: the speeches of genocidal leaders, hunger as a weapon of war…”
« Je pense qu’ il y a de la lâcheté poli: “I think there is political and moral cowardice,” he drops.
Et à ceux qui attendent encore une recon: And to those who are still waiting for formal recognition, what does he say? Mr. Kalinda is categorical: “Journalists who say they’re waiting… will be waiting a long time. The jurists will split hairs.”
<strong>« On ne se pose plus la question: “We’re no longer asking whether it’s genocide; we’re asking about guilt, complicity, failure to denounce genocide”
Quelques rédactions, toutefois, ont choi: A few newsrooms, however, have chosen to call the massacres in Gaza a genocide, including those of L’Humanité, Médiapart and Blast.
La Converse a communiqué avec les direct: La Converse contacted the editorial leadership of these three outlets, but at the time of writing, none of them had responded to our interview requests. We were, however, able to speak with Jérôme Hourdeaux, a journalist at Médiapart.
« Pour moi, le tournant, c’était au mois: “For me, the turning point was in December 2024. First,<l1> Amnesty International</l1>, then <l2>Médecins Sans Frontières</l2> released report after report saying that there was no longer a risk of genocide, but that there was a genocide,” he begins.
Dès la première semaine qui suit le 7 oc: From the first week after October 7, 2023, the Médiapart team asked itself: what is the international community really witnessing? How should it be named?
À l’époque, les tensions politiques sont: At the time, political tensions ran high, particularly around questions of semantics. Many French commentators, Jérôme Hourdeaux explains, demanded that their interviewees describe Hamas’s attacks as “terrorist,” glossing over Israel’s deadly strikes on Gaza in the process. Those who did not play along risked being labelled “complacent,” he reports.
« On s’est vite rendu compte qu’il y ava: “We quickly realized there were a lot of political stakes around these terms, particularly in France,” the journalist explains. The newsroom therefore turned to international lawyers to ask them which international offences apply to the situation, and to understand: what is a crime against humanity, a war crime, a genocide?
« Et donc, après, c’est la ligne qu’on a: “And so, after that, it's the line we've always tried to hold,” explains Mr. Hourdeaux.
Pourtant cette désignation est loin de f: Yet this designation is far from unanimous, which exasperates the journalist: “I think describing the facts is now enough to describe the offence. [All the more so] since the Israeli plan is clear; they own it, they state it in declarations that are sometimes even outrageous. (...) In recent weeks, we're not only sure that there is a genocide, but we also believe that not calling it that is a mistake,” he sighs.
Cette omission est loin d’être neutre, a: This omission is far from neutral, the journalist adds. “Since the term is on the table, when a newsroom doesn't use it, it necessarily means something,” he says. “It means that they refuse to use it.”
Pour M. Hourdeaux, le débat ne porte plu: For Mr. Hourdeaux, the debate is no longer about the designation itself, but about the responsibility of those who continue not to use it, he notes.
« L’Histoire jugera. Dans 20 ou 30 ans,: “History will judge. In 20 or 30 years, when we have some historical distance from what happened in Gaza and compare what the press was saying at the time, it may have the same effect as with other periods of history, when we realized that the press had supported authoritarian regimes or regimes responsible for war crimes. And then, yes, some people may not be proud,” concludes the Mediapart journalist.
Pour Maxime Cochelin, journaliste de Bla: For Maxime Cochelin, a journalist at Blast, the use of the term “genocide” is the result of a clear-eyed examination of what is happening on the ground, carried out in light of the law.
« C’est la lecture même de la Convention: “It's simply a reading of the United Nations Genocide Convention, combined with a minimum of intellectual honesty and backed up, what's more, by the statements of Ilan Pappé, Omer Bartov, Omer Shatz, Francesca Albanese, Amnesty International and so many other figures, including many from the Palestinian community,” he explains.
Mais au-delà de ces choix éditoriaux ou: But beyond these editorial or individual choices, a broader question arises: that of the power of the traditional press in the face of social media.
Carla Murphy, professeure de journalisme: Carla Murphy, a journalism professor at Rutgers University in New Jersey who specializes in media ethics and social justice issues, sees a profound change in how people get their information.
« Je ne suis pas certaine que l’usage ou: “I'm not sure that the use or non-use of the word ‘genocide' by traditional media still matters as much. « [Il] a aujourd’hui accès à la définiti: “[The public] now has access to the UN definition of genocide, to reports from Amnesty and other NGOs. « Bien sûr que c’est important pour une: “Of course it matters for a democracy to have transparent, rigorous journalism. But I'm not sure audiences still recognize its value.”
Depuis Gaza, Rami, lui, constate un « pe: From Gaza, Rami, for his part, sees a “small awakening” in Western French-language media on the subject of the genocide in Gaza. “You can see that they're a bit more willing to talk about massacres, to ask whether or not there is a genocide… At least they're starting to use the word.” This “small awakening” has not gone unnoticed by him.
Lorsqu’on lui demande s’il envisage de q: Asked whether he would consider leaving Gaza if the massacres were to end, his answer is clear: “I'd like to get out, to get a bit of a change of air with my family, I promised my children… But leaving Gaza for good, no, that's not the plan… unless I'm forced to, if I'm forced to move south, if I'm forced onto a ship, if I'm expelled to another country.
